passages.t: The twelve sent out, and Herod's question
passages.happening:
Jesus calls the twelve together and gives them “power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases” (verse 1). He sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick.

They are to take nothing with them: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. They are to stay in whatever house welcomes them. Where they are not welcomed, they are to shake the dust off their feet as they leave. So they go from village to village, preaching and healing everywhere.

News of all this reaches Herod, the ruler of Galilee. People are saying that John has risen from the dead, or that Elijah has appeared, or one of the old prophets. Herod is puzzled. “I beheaded John,” he says, “but who is this man I hear such things about?” (verse 9). And he keeps trying to see Jesus.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells the sending too (Mark 6:7-13), and the note there explains it. Travelling with nothing meant depending on the people who took you in. Staying in one house showed that the disciples were not shopping around for a better host. Shaking the dust off your feet was a public sign of breaking off, as Paul and Barnabas later did (Acts 13:51).

Luke tells it more briefly, and with one difference worth seeing. In Mark the disciples may take a walking stick; in Luke and Matthew they may not (Matthew 10:10). The Gospel writers pass on the same instruction in slightly different forms, and the point in each is the same: go light, and trust God.

Herod here is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee under Rome. Mark tells at length how he had John the Baptist killed (Mark 6:14-29). Luke gives only Herod's own blunt words, ‘I beheaded John’, and his question. It is the question the whole chapter is about: who is this? Herod's wish to see Jesus is paid off much later, at the trial, when he finally meets him and hopes to see a miracle (23:8).
passages.ot: The crowd's guesses come from Scripture. The prophet Malachi had promised, “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). So when a man of power appeared, Elijah was a natural name to reach for. Elijah will come back in this chapter more than once: on the mountain (verse 30), and in the disciples' wish to call down fire (verse 54).
passages.hard: Why does Luke not tell the story of John's death, as Mark does? He does not say. Luke has already told his readers that Herod locked John in prison (3:19-20), and he keeps his story moving toward Jesus. For Luke, the important thing is not how John died but the question his death raised in Herod's mind. Curiosity about Jesus is not the same as faith. Herod wants to see him, as one might want to see a famous man, but nothing in Luke suggests he wants to follow him.
passages.asks: The twelve were sent with power, but without supplies. They had to depend on God and on the kindness of strangers. Ask what you hold on to so that you never have to depend on anyone. And ask Herod's question honestly: who is this man? Wanting to see Jesus is a start. Luke is about to show what it means to follow him.

passages.happening:
The apostles come back and tell Jesus what they have done. He takes them away privately toward a town called Bethsaida. But the crowds find out and follow. Jesus welcomes them, speaks to them about the kingdom of God, and heals those who need it.

Late in the day the twelve say, “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding villages and countryside for lodging and provisions” (verse 12). Jesus answers, “You give them something to eat” (verse 13). They have only five loaves and two fish. There are about five thousand men.

Jesus has the people sit in groups of about fifty. He takes the loaves and fish, looks up to heaven, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to the disciples to set before the people. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets of pieces are left over.
passages.hearers:
It is one of the few events told in all four Gospels. Mark's note explains the setting (Mark 6:30-44): a crowd far from food, a sum of money far beyond what the disciples had, and only the men counted, so the crowd was larger still (Matthew 14:21).

Luke's version has its own touches. Jesus ‘welcomed’ the crowd, though he had gone away to be alone with his friends. And Luke names Bethsaida, a fishing town near where the Jordan runs into the north end of the lake. Its exact site is still argued over by archaeologists.

Right after this, Luke goes straight to Peter's confession. In Mark a long stretch of stories comes between the two (Mark 6:45 to 8:26): Jesus walking on the water, arguments about what makes a person unclean, a Gentile woman, a second feeding. Luke has none of them here. No one knows for sure why. The effect is that the feeding and the question ‘Who do you say I am?’ stand side by side.
passages.ot:
God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness: “Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day” (Exodus 16:4). The groups of fifty recall how Moses set leaders over Israel in groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (Exodus 18:21). And the prophet Elisha once fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, saying, “They will eat and have some left over” (2 Kings 4:43).

The four actions, took, blessed, broke and gave, come back twice more in Luke: at the Last Supper (22:19) and at the meal in Emmaus, where the risen Jesus is recognised “in the breaking of the bread” (24:35).
passages.hard: Some have explained the miracle away. Perhaps, they say, people had food hidden in their clothes, and one person's example made them share. It is a kind thought, but it is not what Luke says. He tells of five loaves that fed thousands, with more left over than there was at the start. A reader may believe it or not, but should not make the text say something gentler than it does.
passages.asks: The disciples' plan was sensible: send the people away. Jesus' answer was, ‘You give them something to eat.’ He did not ask for more than they had. He asked for what they had, and then he blessed it. Ask what small thing you have been holding back because it seems too little to matter. And notice who handed out the bread: the same disciples who had wanted to send everyone home.

passages.happening:
One day Jesus is praying alone, with only his disciples near him. He asks them, “Who do the crowds say I am?” (verse 18). They give the same answers Herod heard: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets come back.

“But what about you?” Jesus asks. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answers, “The Christ of God” (verse 20).

Jesus strictly warns them not to tell anyone. Then he says, “The Son of Man must suffer many things” (verse 22). He must be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised to life.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this too, at Caesarea Philippi in the far north (Mark 8:27-30; Matthew 16:13-20), and their notes explain the place and the word. ‘Christ’ is the Greek form of the Hebrew Messiah. Both mean ‘anointed one’, a person marked out by God for a task, as kings were anointed with oil. Many Jews of the time hoped for a king from David's family who would drive out the foreign rulers.

Luke leaves out the place. Instead he says Jesus was praying. Luke often shows Jesus praying at the turning points: at his baptism (3:21), before he chose the twelve (6:12), and here, before the question that changes everything.

Luke also leaves out what comes next in Mark: Peter's protest and Jesus' words, ‘Get behind Me, Satan’ (Mark 8:32-33). Luke goes straight from the confession to the cross. The title is right. Now Jesus shows what kind of Christ he is.
passages.ot:
God promised David a son whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and a psalm calls the king God's ‘Anointed One’ (Psalm 2:2). Peter's words mean: you are that king.

‘Must’ in verse 22 is a word Luke uses for what God's plan requires. After the resurrection Jesus will explain it from the whole of Scripture: “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (24:26).
passages.hard: Why tell them to keep quiet? The note on Mark 8:27-30 gives the most common answer. The title was true, but most people had the wrong picture of it. If word spread that the Messiah had come, crowds would expect a war against Rome. Jesus first shows them what his kind of kingship costs: rejection, death, and only then the rising.
passages.asks: Jesus moves from ‘What do the crowds say?’ to ‘What about you?’ It is easy to report other people's opinions about Jesus. He asks for yours. Who do you say he is? And are you ready for his answer to follow at once: a Christ who suffers?

passages.happening:
Then Jesus speaks to all of them: “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me” (verse 23).

Whoever wants to save his life will lose it. Whoever loses his life for Jesus' sake will save it. “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self?” (verse 25). If anyone is ashamed of Jesus and his words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in glory.

And Jesus adds, “some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew have these words too (Mark 8:34 to 9:1; Matthew 16:24-28), and the note on Mark 8 explains the cross. To Jesus' hearers it was not a picture of any small trouble. It was Rome's death for slaves and rebels, and a condemned man carried his own cross to the place where he would die. It was meant to shame as well as to kill.

Luke adds one word that Mark and Matthew do not have: daily. Mark says ‘take up his cross’. Luke says ‘take up his cross daily’. The cross is still a matter of life and death. But Luke makes it the shape of an ordinary day, not only of one great moment. Each morning a follower says no again to self as master, and yes to Jesus.

Luke also says ‘his very self’ where Mark speaks of the soul. The meaning is the same: you can win everything and lose the person you are.
passages.ot: A psalm asks what anyone could pay to buy back a life: “For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice” (Psalm 49:8). Jesus asks the same question in the language of trade. The ‘Son of Man’ coming in glory points to Daniel's vision of one like a son of man, given everlasting rule (Daniel 7:13-14).
passages.hard:
Does ‘deny himself’ mean hating yourself, or accepting whatever harm others do to you? No. It means saying no to self as master. The self is not destroyed; it is handed over to Christ, and Jesus promises that it is saved, not lost. The cross he speaks of is carried for his sake. It is not suffering that another person forces on you. If someone is hurting you, seeking safety is not a failure to carry your cross.

What of verse 27? The note on Mark 9:1-8 sets out how Christians have read it: as pointing to the glory on the mountain eight days later, or to the resurrection and the coming of the Spirit, or to both. Luke's wording is simpler than Mark's. They will ‘see the kingdom of God’, and the very next scene shows three of them seeing its glory.
passages.asks: Jesus says ‘daily’. Following him is not only a choice made once at a church meeting. It is made again on an ordinary Tuesday. Ask what saying no to yourself would look like tomorrow morning: in a word held back, a plan given up, a kindness that costs. And ask what you are trying to gain that might cost you your very self.

passages.t: Glory on the mountain, and the talk of his departure
passages.happening:
About eight days later Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray. As he is praying, his face changes and his clothes become dazzling white.

Two men appear and talk with him: Moses and Elijah. They appear in glory and speak about “His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (verse 31).

Peter and the others have been heavy with sleep. When they wake, they see Jesus' glory and the two men. As Moses and Elijah are leaving, Peter offers to put up three shelters. Luke adds, “He did not know what he was saying” (verse 33). A cloud covers them, and they are afraid. A voice comes from the cloud: “This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!” (verse 35). Then Jesus is alone. The disciples keep quiet and tell no one what they have seen.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this too (Mark 9:2-8; Matthew 17:1-8). The note on Mark 9 explains the shelters, which recall the huts of the Feast of Tabernacles, and the mountain, which no Gospel names. Christians since the 200s have pointed to Mount Tabor; many modern scholars suggest Mount Hermon. No one can be sure.

Only Luke tells us three things. First, Jesus went up to pray, and was changed while he was praying. Second, Moses and Elijah talked with him about his ‘departure’. The Greek word is exodos, the same word that gave the book of Exodus its name. It is used only three times in the New Testament, and the other two are about Israel leaving Egypt (Hebrews 11:22) and about Peter's coming death (2 Peter 1:15). Jesus' death, and all that follows it, will be a new exodus: God's great rescue of his people. Third, the disciples were heavy with sleep, as they will be again in the garden on the night of his arrest (22:45).

The voice says ‘whom I have chosen’, where Mark and Matthew have ‘beloved’. The oldest copies of Luke have ‘chosen’. Many later copies changed it to ‘beloved’ to match the other Gospels, and the King James Version follows them.
passages.ot:
Almost everything here looks back to Moses on Mount Sinai: a mountain, a cloud, a voice, and a shining face. When Moses came down from Sinai, “his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD” (Exodus 34:29). Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets, the whole of Israel's Scripture.

The voice joins three passages. “You are My Son” comes from a psalm about God's king (Psalm 2:7). ‘Chosen’ recalls God's servant in Isaiah: “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights” (Isaiah 42:1). And ‘Listen to Him’ echoes Moses' promise of a prophet to come: “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15).
passages.hard: Why was the glory shown, and why so briefly? One common answer is that it was given to strengthen the disciples for the cross. Jesus had just told them he must suffer and die. Now three of them see who he truly is, so that when they see him beaten and crucified they will have something to remember. Peter wanted to stay. But the glory does not stay on the mountain. It goes down with Jesus to a crowd, a sick boy and, in the end, to Jerusalem.
passages.asks: The heavenly visitors did not talk about how wonderful the moment was. They talked about Jerusalem and the death that waited there. And the voice did not say ‘Look at him’ but ‘Listen to him’. Ask whether you want the bright moments of faith more than the words of Jesus. What has he said that you would rather not hear?

passages.happening:
The next day, as they come down the mountain, a large crowd meets Jesus. A man shouts, “Teacher, I beg You to look at my son, for he is my only child” (verse 38). A spirit seizes the boy. He screams, goes into convulsions and foams at the mouth. The father begged the disciples to drive it out, and they could not.

“O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus says. “How long must I remain with you and put up with you? Bring your son here” (verse 41). Even as the boy comes, he is thrown to the ground. Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit, heals the boy, and gives him back to his father. Everyone is amazed at the greatness of God.

While they are all marvelling, Jesus tells his disciples, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men” (verse 44). They do not understand. The meaning is hidden from them, and they are afraid to ask.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story at greater length (Mark 9:14-29; Matthew 17:14-21), and the note on Mark 9 explains it. The boy's attacks sound to many modern readers like what we now call epilepsy. Ancient people knew seizures too; a Greek medical writing from about 400 BC argued that they have natural causes. Mark keeps the father's honest prayer, ‘I do believe; help my unbelief.’

Luke's version is shorter and gentler. Only Luke says the boy was the man's only child. Luke has done this before: the widow of Nain's only son (7:12), and Jairus's only daughter (8:42). And only Luke says that Jesus ‘gave him back to his father’, the same words he used at Nain (7:15). Luke wants us to see a father's fear, and a Lord who gives children back.

The second warning about Jesus' death comes in the middle of the crowd's praise. Glory, and then the cross, again.
passages.ot: ‘Unbelieving and perverse generation’ echoes Moses' song about Israel in the wilderness, “a perverse and crooked generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5). Jesus speaks as Moses did, grieved at a people slow to trust God. ‘Gave him back’ to his father recalls Elijah, who gave the widow's son back to his mother (1 Kings 17:23).
passages.hard:
Does this story mean that seizures, or illness of the mind, are caused by demons? Christians hold that evil is real, and the Gospels tell of real possession. But most Christians today hold that seizures and mental illness are illnesses, to be treated with medicine and care, and that it is wrong and harmful to tell a sick person they have a demon. The Gospels themselves know the difference.

Whom is Jesus rebuking with ‘O unbelieving and perverse generation’? Not the desperate father, who did exactly the right thing in bringing his son. The words are a cry of grief over a whole generation, the disciples included, who had been given power (9:1) and still could not help.
passages.asks: The father had already asked for help and been let down by Jesus' own followers. He asked again anyway. If you have asked the church for help and found it powerless, Luke does not hide that this happens. But the story does not end with the disciples. It ends with Jesus saying, ‘Bring your son here.’ What do you need to bring to him again, even after you have been let down?

passages.t: Who is the greatest? Not one of us
passages.happening:
An argument starts among the disciples about which of them is the greatest. Jesus knows what they are thinking. He takes a little child and stands the child beside him.

“Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me,” he says, “and whoever welcomes Me welcomes the One who sent Me. For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest” (verse 48).

“Master,” says John, “we saw someone driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us” (verse 49). “Do not stop him,” Jesus replies, “for whoever is not against you is for you” (verse 50).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew both tell these scenes (Mark 9:33-41; Matthew 18:1-5), and their notes explain them. A small child in that world was loved but had no rank. A child could not give orders or pay anyone back. Greek even used one word, pais, for a child and for a servant. To welcome a child gained you nothing.

Luke's telling sits sharply against what came just before. The disciples could not heal the boy. They did not understand Jesus' words about his death. Now they argue about rank, and then they try to stop a man who was succeeding where they had failed. Luke lets the four failures stand in a row.

Luke has Jesus stand the child ‘beside him’, as if in a place of honour. The least is put next to the Lord.
passages.ot: Something like John's complaint happened to Moses. Two men prophesied outside the camp, and Joshua wanted them stopped. Moses answered, “Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29).
passages.hard: Later in Luke, Jesus says the opposite: “He who is not with Me is against Me” (11:23). Do the two clash? The note on Mark 9:38-41 answers that they speak to different situations. Here, someone is doing good in Jesus' name, though not in the disciples' circle: leave him alone. In chapter 11, Jesus speaks of people who call his work the devil's: there is no neutral ground toward Jesus himself. Be generous toward others who serve Jesus; be honest about where you stand toward Jesus.
passages.asks: John's objection was ‘he does not accompany us’. Not ‘he does not follow You’. Ask where you have treated your own church, group or tradition as the edge of God's work. And ask who the ‘little child’ is in your world: the person who can do nothing for you. Jesus says that welcoming them is welcoming him.

passages.t: His face set toward Jerusalem; fire refused
passages.happening:
“As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem” (verse 51). He sends messengers ahead into a Samaritan village to get things ready. But the people there will not welcome him, because he is heading for Jerusalem.

James and John see it and ask, “Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?” (verse 54). “But Jesus turned and rebuked them” (verse 55). And they go on to another village.
passages.hearers:
This is the turning point of Luke's book. The book page shows it: from here until he reaches the city in chapter 19, Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, and Luke keeps reminding us (13:22, 17:11, 18:31). Much of what only Luke has, the Good Samaritan, the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, is told along this road.

The Greek of verse 51 says, word for word, that ‘he set his face to go to Jerusalem’. The BSB puts it as ‘resolutely set out’. It means a firm decision, made knowing what waits there. ‘Ascension’ translates a Greek word, analēmpsis, found only here in the New Testament. It means ‘being taken up’. Luke uses the verb from the same root for Jesus going up to heaven (Acts 1:2). So the road leads to the cross, and through it to the resurrection and to the Father.

The Samaritans lived in the hill country between Galilee and Judea. The note on John 4 explains who they were. They worshipped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but at their own mountain, Gerizim, not at Jerusalem. Bad feeling ran deep on both sides, and had a long history. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of Galilean pilgrims killed at a Samaritan village on their way to a feast (Antiquities 20.118). So a village that would not help a band of Galileans going to Jerusalem was doing something people expected. The Samaritans are not only people in an old story: a small Samaritan community, about nine hundred people, still lives today and keeps its faith.
passages.ot:
James and John are thinking of Elijah. When a king sent soldiers to arrest him, Elijah said, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men” (2 Kings 1:10), and it did. The disciples have just seen Elijah on the mountain. They think they know what a prophet does to people who refuse him.

‘Set his face’ is the language of the prophets. Isaiah's servant of God says, “therefore I have set My face like flint, and I know that I will not be put to shame” (Isaiah 50:7).
passages.hard:
Jesus rebukes the wish for fire. Whatever Elijah once did, Jesus will not destroy people for refusing him, and he does not let his followers do it in his name. This passage can never be a warrant for violence against anyone in God's name: not against a village, a people, a religion, or a person who says no to Jesus. The people who refused him were simply passed by. Later in Luke a Samaritan becomes the hero of Jesus' most famous story (10:33), and a Samaritan is the one leper who comes back to thank him (17:16). In Acts the good news is welcomed in Samaria (Acts 8:5-6).

Some Bibles, such as the King James Version, have more words here. In verse 54 they add ‘as Elijah did’. In verses 55 and 56 they add Jesus' words, ‘You do not know what kind of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them.’ The oldest copies, among them a papyrus from around AD 200 (P75) and the great Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have these words. Some later copies have part of them, and many have all. Most scholars think they were added by copyists to explain the rebuke, and so modern Bibles put them in a footnote. They are true to Jesus, who says in Luke that he came “to seek and to save the lost” (19:10). But the plainer text is enough: Jesus turned and rebuked them.
passages.asks: Two disciples met rejection and reached for fire. It is an old temptation, to answer people who refuse us, or refuse our faith, with anger and punishment. Jesus turned to his own followers and rebuked them, and then simply walked on. Ask where you have wanted fire to fall on someone who said no. And notice where Jesus was going while they argued: to Jerusalem, to be rejected himself.

passages.happening:
As they walk along the road, someone says, “I will follow You wherever You go” (verse 57). Jesus answers, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head” (verse 58).

Jesus says to another man, “Follow Me.” He answers, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father” (verse 59). Jesus says, “Let the dead bury their own dead. You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God” (verse 60).

A third says, “I will follow You, Lord; but first let me bid farewell to my family” (verse 61). Jesus answers, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (verse 62).
passages.hearers:
Matthew tells the first two of these meetings (Matthew 8:18-22), and the note there explains them. ‘The Son of Man’ was Jesus' favourite way of speaking of himself. The one Daniel saw receiving an everlasting kingdom has nowhere to sleep tonight. In Luke the words land with extra weight: Jesus has just been refused a bed by a Samaritan village.

Burying your father was one of the most sacred duties a Jewish son had. What exactly the man was asking is not certain. His father may just have died. He may have been asking to wait for a second burial, when a family gathered the bones into a stone box a year or so later. Or his father may still have been alive, and he meant, ‘Let me wait until he dies.’ On any reading, Jesus claims a loyalty that comes before even the most honoured family duty.

Only Luke has the third man, and only Luke adds ‘go and proclaim the kingdom of God’. The call is not only to leave something but to go and do something.

A plough was pulled by oxen, and the man guiding it had to look ahead to cut a straight line. If he looked back over his shoulder, the furrow went crooked.
passages.ot: The third man's request echoes Elisha. When Elijah called him from his ploughing, Elisha said, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you” (1 Kings 19:20), and Elijah let him go. Jesus asks for more than Elijah did. And the picture of the plough comes from the same story: Elisha was ploughing with twelve teams of oxen when the call came (1 Kings 19:19).
passages.hard:
‘Let the dead bury their own dead’ is one of the hardest things Jesus said, and it should not be softened. Most readers take ‘the dead’ to mean people who are not following Jesus, who are dead to the life he brings: let them see to it. The call to follow him cannot wait.

But it is not contempt for family. Jesus rebuked people who used religion as an excuse not to care for their parents (Mark 7:10-13), and in Luke he names “Honor your father and mother” among the commandments (18:20). On the cross he made sure his mother would be cared for (John 19:26-27). These words were spoken to one man at one moment, about what comes first. They do not tell anyone to stay away from a parent's funeral or to abandon a parent who needs care. Caring for an aging or dying parent is part of obeying Jesus, not a rival to it.

If you are grieving a father or mother now, hear this clearly: grief is not disobedience. Jesus himself grieved.
passages.asks: Each of the three had a ‘but first’, or would soon find one. Comfort, duty, the people at home. None of these is bad, which is what makes them hard. Ask what your ‘but first’ is. Is there something you call a duty that has become a way of saying ‘not yet’? And ask what ‘go and proclaim’ might mean for you, where you already are.
